nodes.title: American 5342 / Black Hawk

nodes.title: SWISS 17K
nodes.label: SWISS 17K
nodes.description: An Airbus A330 was cleared for takeoff at JFK just before a second controller cleared four aircraft to cross its runway.
nodes.creator: Markus Eigenheer from Genève, Schweiz

nodes.title: FedEx 1432 / Southwest 708
nodes.label: FedEx / Southwest
nodes.description: In dense fog at Austin, FedEx 1432 continued its approach as Southwest 708 was cleared to take off on the same runway.
nodes.creator: Acroterion

nodes.title: American 106 / Delta 1943
nodes.label: American / Delta
nodes.description: American 106 missed a taxiway turn and crossed an active JFK runway as Delta 1943 began its takeoff roll.
nodes.creator: Alan Wilson

nodes.title: Air Canada 726 / Air Canada 1259
nodes.label: Air Canada 726
nodes.description: Air Canada 726 taxied onto an active runway at Toronto Pearson while Air Canada 1259 was on final approach.
nodes.creator: Charles from Port Chester, New York

nodes.title: Comair 5191
nodes.label: Comair 5191
nodes.description: Cleared for runway 22 at Lexington, Comair 5191 turned onto the much shorter runway 26 and began its takeoff.
nodes.creator: NTSB

nodes.title: SAS 686 / D-IEVX
nodes.label: SAS 686

nodes.creator: Ken Fielding (Flickr)

nodes.title: United 1448 / FedEx 1662

nodes.title: USAir 1493 / SkyWest 5569

nodes.creator: Anders Nilsson

nodes.title: Northwest 1482 / Northwest 299

nodes.creator: Hawaiian897

edges.evidence: Marine One’s calls to DCA tower were not received or were unreadable because radio coverage lacked line of sight to The Ellipse.
After a traffic advisory Marine One immediately reported the airliner in sight.
The system relied too much on pilot-applied visual separation, and the helicopter crew did not apply it effectively.
The tower team lost situation awareness, leading to inadequate traffic advisories and no safety alerts.
A 0.8-second transmission blocked the “pass behind” part of the controller’s instruction.
Four aircraft crossed runway 4L while SWISS 17K was taking off.
A takeoff clearance and a crossing clearance for runway 4L were given one second apart.
Dense fog stopped the controller seeing the 737.
The FAA did not require surface detection equipment at Austin.
The controller lacked awareness of the 737’s position when it asked for takeoff.
The NTSB classed the event as a runway incursion.
American 106 crossed runway 4L without clearance as Delta 1943 took off.
The distraction led to a loss of situational awareness.
ACA726 taxied across the hold line onto Runway 24R without authorization while ACA1259 was on final.
Plain-language taxi instruction was misinterpreted and the same-phraseology readback did not confirm common understanding.
Taxiing onto and taking off from runway 26 without clearance made the accident a runway incursion.
The conversation during taxi resulted in a loss of positional awareness on the airport surface.
ANSV names the Cessna’s entry onto the active runway as the immediate cause.
Fog limited visibility to 50 to 100 metres, listed among the causes.
The ground movement radar was out of service and controllers had no technical aids to confirm positions.
The Providence tower had no surface detection equipment.
Visibility was 1/4 mile at night.
United 1448 was near an active runway while FedEx 1662 departed.
The controller cleared the 737 to land on the runway where she had placed the Metroliner.
SkyWest 5569 was in position on runway 24L when USAir 1493 landed on it.
The lost DC-9 taxied onto runway 3C during the 727’s takeoff roll.
Dense fog, with visibility estimated as low as about 100 ft near the collision.
Pan Am was still taxiing on the runway, and KLM did not stop when Pan Am reported this (corrected translation).
The tower’s “stand by for take-off” and Pan Am’s “still taxiing” call were transmitted at the same time, causing a whistle of about three seconds.
Low cloud blowing across the airport made visibility change suddenly between near zero and about 1 km.
